If automatic officiating equipment is available, the referee reviews the relevant footage to verify the disqualification; the referee and starter need not agree in that review route.
rulebook.plain: An early start requires the applicable observation or footage-review process. Joint visual confirmation and automatic-footage review are different routes.

rulebook.title: Other breaches: report and referee decision
rulebook.statement: The referee must disqualify for another breach personally witnessed by the referee, and may disqualify on another technical official’s verbal breach report. After the referee confirms the disqualification, the reporting official completes and signs a card specifying the event, lane and infraction.
rulebook.plain: The reporting official supplies the observed facts; the referee confirms the decision, followed by the signed card.

rulebook.title: Assigning relay take-off observers
rulebook.statement: The referee appoints technical officials to judge whether the next swimmer’s feet still contact the platform when the incoming teammate touches to complete their quarter of the relay distance.
rulebook.plain: Assigned officials compare the incoming relay touch with the outgoing swimmer’s platform contact.

rulebook.title: Supervising electronic officiating equipment
rulebook.statement: The control-room supervisor oversees operation of the automatic and/or semi-automatic officiating equipment used at the meet.
rulebook.plain: The control-room supervisor oversees the electronic officiating systems.

rulebook.title: Checking results and relay exchanges
rulebook.statement: The control-room supervisor checks computer result outputs and the relay-exchange printout, and reports any early relay take-off to the referee.
rulebook.plain: Check the result and relay timing records, then report early take-offs to the referee.

rulebook.title: Optional video-timing check of relay take-offs
rulebook.statement: The control-room supervisor may examine video timing to confirm an early relay take-off.
rulebook.plain: Video timing can be checked when confirming a suspected early takeover.

rulebook.title: Control-room results administration
rulebook.statement: The control-room supervisor handles withdrawals following heats or semi-finals, enters results on official forms, lists newly established records and, where applicable, maintains award scoring under Part One 11.
rulebook.plain: The control room also handles withdrawals, official result records, new records and applicable award scores.

rulebook.title: Starter control after the referee’s handover
rulebook.statement: Once the referee transfers control under Part Two 4.1 or 4.2, the starter controls the swimmers until racing begins and conducts the start using Article 4.
rulebook.plain: The starter takes over from the referee for the starting procedure.

rulebook.title: Delaying or disobeying at the start
rulebook.statement: The starter reports a swimmer’s delay, deliberate disobedience of a starter instruction or other start misconduct to the referee. The referee may disqualify that swimmer.
rulebook.plain: Start misconduct is reported to the referee, who may disqualify the swimmer.

rulebook.title: Fair-start decision and recall
rulebook.statement: The starter decides whether a start was fair, subject to the referee’s decision. An unfair start results in recall of the swimmers and a restart.
rulebook.plain: The starter judges fairness under the referee’s authority; an unfair start is recalled and restarted.
rulebook.issue: This fairness/recall provision is separate from Article 4.4.1, which lets a race continue when the signal preceded declaration of an individual early-start disqualification.

rulebook.title: Starter position and signal visibility
rulebook.statement: For the start, the starter stands at the poolside within approximately 5 metres of the starting end. The position must let timekeepers see and/or hear the signal and let swimmers hear it.
rulebook.plain: The starter stands near the start end where swimmers can hear the signal and timekeepers can see or hear it.

rulebook.title: Starter reports observed breaches
rulebook.statement: The starter reports any observed false start or other breach to the referee.
rulebook.plain: The starter reports what they observe to the referee.

rulebook.title: Call-room assembly, absence and equipment concerns
rulebook.statement: Call-room judges assemble swimmers before each race. They report possible swimwear or advertising breaches, and any swimmer absent when called, to the call-room supervisor. The supervisor decides whether the swimwear or advertising rules were breached and reports a confirmed breach to the referee.
rulebook.plain: Call-room staff assemble swimmers and raise absence or kit concerns. The supervisor assesses kit-rule concerns before reporting a breach.

rulebook.title: Chief inspector supervises turn inspectors
rulebook.statement: The chief inspector of turns ensures the turn inspectors carry out their duties during the competition.
rulebook.plain: The chief inspector oversees the turn-inspection team.

rulebook.title: Turn inspectors for every lane at both ends
rulebook.statement: One inspector is assigned to each lane at each end to check the relevant requirements following the start, at every turn and at the finish.
rulebook.plain: Turn inspectors watch their lane’s starts, turns and finishes from the two ends.

rulebook.title: Turn-inspector observation after a start
rulebook.statement: At the starting end, the inspector’s remit runs from the starting signal through completion of the first arm stroke. In breaststroke it extends through completion of the second arm stroke instead.
rulebook.plain: The start check includes the first arm stroke, or the second in breaststroke.

rulebook.title: Turn-inspector observation around a turn
rulebook.statement: The turn-inspection period starts when the last arm stroke before contact begins and ends when the first outgoing arm stroke is complete. In breaststroke the period ends after completion of the second outgoing arm stroke.
rulebook.plain: Watch the incoming final stroke, contact and outgoing first stroke; breaststroke coverage continues through the second outgoing stroke.

rulebook.title: Turn-inspector observation at a finish
rulebook.statement: An inspector’s finish remit begins at the start of the last arm stroke before the swimmer touches the wall.
rulebook.plain: The finish check begins with the final arm stroke, before contact.

rulebook.title: Installing and removing a backstroke ledge
rulebook.statement: Where a backstroke ledge is used, the starting-end inspector installs and removes the ledge in their lane. The ledge is set to zero after installation.
rulebook.plain: The lane’s inspector fits the ledge at the zero setting and removes it.

rulebook.title: Lap counting and lap cards in distance freestyle
rulebook.statement: In individual 400 m, 800 m and 1500 m freestyle, inspectors at both ends record the laps completed in their lanes. At the turning end, odd-numbered lap cards show the laps remaining. The local organising committee selects deck-level or in-water display according to venue availability. Electronic displays, including underwater ones, may serve the same purpose.
rulebook.plain: For these distance races, officials count laps and show the remaining odd-numbered laps at the far end. The display may be physical or electronic.

rulebook.title: Distance-freestyle warning signal
rulebook.statement: In individual 400 m, 800 m and 1500 m freestyle, the starting-end inspector signals when their swimmer has 2 laps plus 5 metres remaining. After the turn the signal is repeated until the swimmer reaches the lane-rope 5-metre mark. A whistle or bell may be used.
rulebook.plain: Give the warning at two laps plus five metres to go, and repeat it after the turn until the swimmer reaches the five-metre mark.

rulebook.title: Inspectors judge relay take-offs
rulebook.statement: At the starting end, inspectors judge whether the outgoing swimmer still contacts the platform at the preceding swimmer’s wall touch. Available automatic equipment designed to assess relay take-offs must also be used.
rulebook.plain: Compare the incoming touch with outgoing platform contact, using available take-off equipment as well.

rulebook.title: Turn inspectors report observed breaches
rulebook.statement: Inspectors report to the referee any breach observed within their remit, including a breach of the applicable stroke rules.
rulebook.plain: An inspector reports observed infractions in their assigned area to the referee.

rulebook.title: Stroke judges on both pool sides
rulebook.statement: Stroke judges are positioned along both sides of the pool.
rulebook.plain: There are stroke judges on each side of the course.

rulebook.title: Stroke judges check action and assist at walls
rulebook.statement: Each stroke judge checks compliance with the event’s swimming-style rules and observes turns and finishes to assist the turn inspectors.
rulebook.plain: Watch the designated stroke and help check the turns and finishes.

rulebook.title: Stroke judges report observed breaches
rulebook.statement: Stroke judges report to the referee any breach they observe within their remit, including a breach of the stroke rules.
rulebook.plain: The stroke judge reports observed infractions to the referee.

rulebook.title: Checking the backstroke flags before racing
rulebook.statement: Before each backstroke or medley event begins, stroke judges ensure the backstroke turn indicators are installed 5 metres from both end walls.
rulebook.plain: Check that the backstroke flags are five metres from each wall before backstroke or medley starts.

rulebook.title: Chief timekeeper assignments and reserves
rulebook.statement: When the chief-timekeeper role is required under 2.1.3, that official assigns the timekeepers’ seats and lanes. Without automatic or semi-automatic officiating equipment, each lane has 2 timekeepers plus at least 1 additional reserve timekeeper for the meet, available when a watch or timekeeper cannot provide a time.
rulebook.plain: Assign seats and lanes; the manual setup needs two timekeepers per lane and at least one reserve.

rulebook.title: Chief timekeeper records the winner
rulebook.statement: When required under 2.1.3, the chief timekeeper must record a time for the winner of every race.
rulebook.plain: The chief timekeeper records a time for each race winner.

rulebook.title: Collecting timing cards and inspecting watches
rulebook.statement: When this role is required under 2.1.3, the chief timekeeper collects each lane’s recorded-time card and checks the timekeepers’ watches if needed.
rulebook.plain: Collect the timing cards and inspect watches when necessary.

rulebook.title: Recording each lane’s official time
rulebook.statement: When this role is required under 2.1.3, the chief timekeeper enters the official time on every lane’s card.
rulebook.plain: The chief timekeeper records the official result on each lane card.

rulebook.title: Timekeeper’s assigned swimmer
rulebook.statement: When timekeepers are required under 2.1.3, each records the swimmer’s time in their assigned lane using the manual-timing rules in Part Two 11.2.
rulebook.plain: Time your assigned lane under the manual-timing procedure.

rulebook.title: Starting, stopping and intermediate times
rulebook.statement: Timekeepers start their watches on the starting signal and stop them when their lane’s swimmer completes the race distance. In races longer than 100 m, they also record intermediate times if the chief timekeeper instructs them to do so.
rulebook.plain: Start on the signal and stop at completion of the distance. Record splits in races over 100 metres when instructed.

rulebook.title: Submitting and resetting watches
rulebook.statement: Immediately after the race, lane timekeepers write down their watch times and give the card to the chief timekeeper. They present watches for inspection if requested. They reset watches on the referee’s short whistles announcing the next race.
rulebook.plain: Write and hand over the times promptly; show the watches if asked. Reset at the next race’s short whistles.

rulebook.title: Timekeepers alongside electronic systems
rulebook.statement: Unless video timing is in use, the full timekeeper complement specified in 2.10 may still be needed even when automatic or semi-automatic officiating equipment is operating.
rulebook.plain: Electronic equipment does not necessarily remove the need for a full timekeeper team; video timing changes this provision.

rulebook.title: Finish judges’ view
rulebook.statement: Where finish judges are used under 2.1.3, they stand in line with the finish and must continuously have a clear view of both the course and finish line.
rulebook.plain: Finish judges need an unobstructed view from the finish line.

rulebook.title: Finish judges report placing
rulebook.statement: After each race, finish judges determine the swimmers’ placing within their assigned tasks and report it to the referee.
rulebook.plain: Report the finishing order covered by your assignment to the referee.

rulebook.title: Separating finish judging from timekeeping
rulebook.statement: A finish judge cannot also act as a timekeeper for the same race, subject to the stated exception for a timekeeper operating semi-automatic officiating equipment under Part Two 15.16.5.
rulebook.plain: Do not combine finish judging and timekeeping in the same race except for the specific semi-automatic-equipment exception.

rulebook.title: Chief recorder checks and witnesses results
rulebook.statement: Outside the Olympic Games and World Aquatics Events, the chief recorder checks results from computer outputs or from the race times and placing supplied by the referee. The chief recorder witnesses the referee signing those results.
rulebook.plain: At the meets covered by this role, check the results and witness the referee’s signature.

rulebook.title: Recorder handles withdrawals and records
rulebook.statement: Outside the Olympic Games and World Aquatics Events, the recorder handles withdrawals after heats or semi-finals, enters results on official forms, lists new records and maintains award scoring under Part One 11 where applicable.
rulebook.plain: At these meets, the recorder handles withdrawals, result paperwork, records and relevant award scores.

rulebook.title: Video-review supervisor keeps judges in post
rulebook.statement: The video-review supervisor ensures the video judges occupy their assigned posts and perform their duties throughout the competition.
rulebook.plain: The supervisor keeps the video-review team in place and working.

rulebook.title: Reviewing video judges’ reports
rulebook.statement: The video-review supervisor reviews and confirms the rule infractions reported by the video-review judges.
rulebook.plain: The supervisor checks reported video-review infractions before they proceed.

rulebook.title: Video review requested by the referee
rulebook.statement: At the referee’s request, the video-review supervisor reviews and confirms the rule infractions referred for that review.
rulebook.plain: The referee can refer reported infractions to the video-review supervisor for checking.

rulebook.title: Reporting confirmed video infractions
rulebook.statement: The video-review supervisor reports every infraction confirmed through video review to the referee.
rulebook.plain: Confirmed video-review infractions go to the referee.

rulebook.title: Video judges check stroke, turns and finishes
rulebook.statement: Video-review judges check compliance with the swimming-style rules designated for the competition and observe turns and finishes.
rulebook.plain: Video judges review swimming action and wall work against the relevant stroke rules.

rulebook.title: Video-review reporting and card route
rulebook.statement: A video judge reports an observed infraction to the video-review supervisor. If confirmed, the judge completes a disqualification card and promptly sends it to the supervisor, who passes it to the referee.
rulebook.plain: A confirmed video infraction follows a clear chain: video judge, supervisor, then referee.

rulebook.title: Resolution desk receives team queries
rulebook.statement: Resolution desk judges are available for team leaders’ initial queries, including withdrawals, disqualifications and swim-offs. They pass those queries to the Technical Swimming Committee commission.
rulebook.plain: Team leaders can take initial queries to the resolution desk, which forwards them to the appropriate commission.

rulebook.title: Supervising competition-pool warm-up
rulebook.statement: Warm-up supervisors oversee warm-up sessions in the competition pool, ensuring the warm-up guidelines are followed and the lanes are used according to their designated purposes.
rulebook.plain: During warm-up, supervisors check the guidelines and assigned lane use.

rulebook.title: Lanes used at the major championships
rulebook.statement: Olympic heats, semi-finals and finals should use eight lanes. At the World Aquatics Championships, World Aquatics Junior Swimming Championships and World Aquatics Swimming Championships (25m), heats may use ten lanes; semi-finals and finals should use eight.
rulebook.plain: Olympic racing normally uses eight lanes. The listed World Aquatics championships can use ten for heats, with eight for the later rounds. These are the stated championship arrangements, not a claim that every pool has eight or ten lanes.

rulebook.title: Heat seeding applies to swimmers and relay teams
rulebook.statement: Heats at the Olympics, World Aquatics events and other competitions conducted under the Competition Regulations allocate both heat and lane by seeding. The following provisions apply to individual swimmers and, through rule 3.2.6, relay teams.
rulebook.plain: Under these rules, recorded times determine your heat and lane; relay teams follow the same heat-seeding framework.

rulebook.title: Enter the fastest competition time
rulebook.statement: The swimmer, or the swimmer’s federation where responsible, must declare the fastest time achieved in competition for the exact stroke and distance. The declaration must use the required paper or online entry form and meet the entry deadline.
rulebook.plain: Enter your fastest competition time for this event, on the correct form and before the deadline.

rulebook.title: Rank entries by their times
rulebook.statement: The management committee collects each entrant’s fastest competition time for the specified stroke and distance, then orders the entries from quickest to slowest.
rulebook.plain: The entry list is sorted by event time, fastest first.

rulebook.title: Missing, late or incorrectly submitted entry time
rulebook.statement: If the fastest competition time is not supplied in the required form by the deadline, the management committee places that swimmer behind all entrants with properly supplied times.
rulebook.plain: A missing or incorrectly submitted time puts you at the end of the seeded entry list.

rulebook.title: Identical entry times
rulebook.statement: When entrants have the same fastest entry time, a random draw determines their order in the ranking.
rulebook.plain: Equal entry times are ordered by a draw.

rulebook.title: One heat becomes a direct final
rulebook.statement: When the number of entrants produces only one heat, that race uses final seeding and is raced as the direct final.
rulebook.plain: With only one race of entrants, you swim a direct final rather than a qualifying heat.

rulebook.title: Two heats: alternate the ranked entries
rulebook.statement: For two heats, distribute entrants in time order using the repeating heat sequence 2, 1. The fastest enters heat 2, second-fastest heat 1, third-fastest heat 2, fourth-fastest heat 1, and so on.
rulebook.plain: The fastest two swimmers are separated: fastest in heat 2, next fastest in heat 1. Continue alternating down the entry list.

rulebook.title: Three heats: distribute across the last three
rulebook.statement: For three heats, other than the 400m, 800m and 1500m events, distribute entrants in time order using the repeating sequence 3, 2, 1. The three fastest therefore enter heats 3, 2 and 1 respectively, and the fourth returns to heat 3.
rulebook.plain: The leading swimmers are spread across three heats: 3, 2, 1, then repeat. Longer-distance exceptions use the separate two-heat arrangement.

rulebook.title: Four or more heats: ordinary-distance arrangement
rulebook.statement: For events other than 400m, 800m and 1500m, four or more heats use the final three heats for the fastest entrants, distributed by the three-heat pattern in 3.2.4.3. The next group fills the immediately preceding heat; progressively slower groups fill the earlier heats under 3.2.4.4.1–3.2.4.4.3.
rulebook.plain: The fastest group is spread over the last three heats. Earlier heats contain progressively slower groups. The 400m, 800m and 1500m have a different arrangement.

rulebook.title: Seed the final three heats
rulebook.statement: In the ordinary-distance arrangement for four or more heats, the quickest entrants assigned to the last three heats alternate in descending heat order: last heat, next-to-last, third-from-last, then repeat. This applies the pattern in 3.2.4.3.
rulebook.plain: Spread the fastest swimmers across the final three heats, working backwards through those heats and repeating.

rulebook.title: Fill the heat before the last three
rulebook.statement: After allocating the quickest entrants across the last three heats, assign the next-fastest group to the heat immediately before those three.
rulebook.plain: The next group of swimmers fills the fourth heat from the end.

rulebook.title: Fill the remaining earlier heats
rulebook.statement: If heats still precede the final four, assign the next-fastest remaining group to the immediately preceding heat and repeat this process backwards through the schedule.
rulebook.plain: Work back towards heat 1, using the next-slowest group each time.

rulebook.title: 400m, 800m and 1500m: seed the last two heats
rulebook.statement: For the 400m, 800m and 1500m, spread the quickest entrants across the final two heats using the alternating pattern in 3.2.4.2: quickest in the last heat, next quickest in the preceding heat, then repeat. If at least three heats are needed, earlier heats receive the remaining groups under 3.2.4.4.5–3.2.4.4.6.
rulebook.plain: For these longer races, spread the top swimmers over the last two heats, not three.
rulebook.issue: The February PDF cites 3.1.3.2, which is an incorrect reference. World Aquatics commentary dated 6 August 2026, PDF p. 1, explicitly corrects it to 3.2.4.2. This restatement uses that published correction. Although the code is nested beneath a paragraph excluding these distances, this clause expressly governs 400m, 800m and 1500m.

rulebook.title: Longer races: fill the heat before the last two
rulebook.statement: In a 400m, 800m or 1500m event requiring three or more heats, the next-fastest group after the swimmers allocated to the final two heats goes into the heat immediately before them.
rulebook.plain: Once the last two longer-distance heats are filled, put the next group in the third heat from the end.

rulebook.title: Longer races: fill earlier heats
rulebook.statement: For 400m, 800m and 1500m events with further earlier heats, place the next-fastest remaining group in the heat before the final three, then continue backwards through any additional heats.
rulebook.plain: Continue filling earlier heats with progressively slower groups.

rulebook.title: Minimum swimmers when seeding heats
rulebook.statement: If an event has at least two heats, each heat must initially be seeded with three or more swimmers. Later withdrawals may leave fewer than three in a heat.
rulebook.plain: Every heat starts with at least three seeded swimmers, but withdrawals can leave a smaller field.

rulebook.title: Lane numbering is viewed from the regular starting end
rulebook.statement: For seeding, face along the pool from its regular starting end. The rightmost lane is numbered 1, except in a ten-lane arrangement where it is 0; numbering increases towards the left. Rule 3.2.5.2 preserves this reference direction even when a 50m race starts at the opposite end.
rulebook.plain: Look down the pool from the normal starting end: lane 1 is on your right, or lane 0 in a ten-lane pool.

rulebook.title: Lane order with an odd number of lanes
rulebook.statement: With an odd lane count, put the fastest swimmer in the middle lane and the second-fastest in its neighbour to the left, viewed from the regular starting end. Continue outwards, alternating right then left. In seven lanes numbered 1–7, the fastest-to-slowest order is 4, 5, 3, 6, 2, 7, 1.
rulebook.plain: Start in the centre and work outwards, left then right in alternating steps. The seven-lane example is 4, 5, 3, 6, 2, 7, 1.

rulebook.title: Lane order in a six-lane pool
rulebook.statement: For six lanes numbered 1–6, assign swimmers from fastest to slowest to lanes 3, 4, 2, 5, 1, 6. This starts with lanes 3 and 4, then alternates outwards on the right and left.
rulebook.plain: Six-lane seeding order: 3, 4, 2, 5, 1, 6.

rulebook.title: Lane order in an eight-lane pool
rulebook.statement: For eight lanes numbered 1–8, assign swimmers from fastest to slowest to lanes 4, 5, 3, 6, 2, 7, 1, 8. This starts with lanes 4 and 5, then alternates outwards on the right and left.
rulebook.plain: Eight-lane seeding order: 4, 5, 3, 6, 2, 7, 1, 8.

rulebook.title: Lane order in a ten-lane pool
rulebook.statement: For ten lanes numbered 0–9, assign swimmers from fastest to slowest to lanes 4, 5, 3, 6, 2, 7, 1, 8, 0, 9. This starts with lanes 4 and 5, then alternates outwards on the right and left.
rulebook.plain: Ten-lane seeding order: 4, 5, 3, 6, 2, 7, 1, 8, 0, 9.

rulebook.title: A draw for unresolved equal seedings
rulebook.statement: Where equally ranked swimmers remain to be assigned and the cited ranking and lane-allocation provisions do not apply, a random draw allocates the next available lanes.
rulebook.plain: If equal seedings still need lane places after the applicable ranking rules, draw the available lanes.
rulebook.issue: The printed condition refers to 3.2.2 and 3.2.5; the latter is the lane-allocation section containing this clause. This entry reports the residual random-draw instruction without inventing an additional tie-break procedure.

rulebook.title: A 50m race may start from either end
rulebook.statement: For a 50m event in a 50m pool, the management committee may choose either direction of racing, taking account of matters such as suitable automatic timing and the starter’s position. Swimmers should be told well in advance. Lane numbers remain fixed by the regular starting end even when swimmers race from the other end; normal seeding still applies.
rulebook.plain: A one-length 50m race can start at either end. The lane numbers do not reverse when the starting end changes.

rulebook.title: Relay heat and lane seeding
rulebook.statement: Relay teams use the entry-time, ranking, heat-allocation and lane-allocation procedures in 3.2.1–3.2.5, treating each team as one entrant.
rulebook.plain: Seed relay teams in heats using the same framework as individual swimmers.

rulebook.title: Seeding the semi-final phase
rulebook.statement: At Olympic, World Aquatics and other competitions governed by these regulations, semi-final heat and lane assignments use the procedures that follow. The printed scope also mentions relay teams, but the August commentary withdraws relay semi-final provision 3.3.5 because World Aquatics relay events have no semi-final round.
rulebook.plain: Individual semi-finalists are seeded into races and lanes. Do not read the old relay reference as requiring relay semi-finals.
rulebook.issue: World Aquatics commentary dated 6 August 2026, PDF p. 1, says relay provision 3.3.5 was included in error and is not applied.

rulebook.title: Distribute qualifiers between two semi-finals
rulebook.statement: Rank qualifiers by their heat times, or by entry times if the event begins directly with semi-finals. Assign them in the repeating semi-final order 2, 1: fastest to semi-final 2, second-fastest to semi-final 1, and continue alternating.
rulebook.plain: The quickest qualifier goes in the second semi-final, the next quickest in the first, then repeat down the list.

rulebook.title: Tie for the last semi-final place at 200m or shorter
rulebook.statement: For an event of 200m or less, swimmers tied in seeding for the final available semi-final place may be asked to race a swim-off to decide who progresses.
rulebook.plain: At 50m, 100m or 200m, a tie for the last semi-final place may be settled by another race.

rulebook.title: Replacing a withdrawn semi-finalist
rulebook.statement: If a semi-finalist withdraws, the management committee admits the fastest previously unqualified swimmer when it considers that reasonably possible. If replacement is made, it re-ranks and re-seeds where practical, redistribute swimmers between semi-finals under 3.3.1, and reassign lanes under 3.3.4.
rulebook.plain: A withdrawal may let the next-fastest reserve in. Officials can then revise the semi-final line-up and lanes where practical.

rulebook.title: Assigning semi-final lanes
rulebook.statement: Use the centre-outwards lane order in 3.2.5.1. When heats have been held, rank swimmers by their official heat times rather than their entry times. Without heats, use the entry-based ranking.
rulebook.plain: Semi-final lanes use the normal centre-out order, based on heat performance if there were heats.

rulebook.title: Relay semi-final clause withdrawn by commentary
rulebook.statement: There is no operative World Aquatics relay semi-final allocation under this clause. The February printing extended 3.3.1–3.3.4 to relay teams, but the August commentary says that insertion was erroneous and is not applied because World Aquatics relay events do not include semi-finals.
rulebook.plain: World Aquatics relay events have no semi-final round. This printed relay semi-final clause has been withdrawn by the later commentary.
rulebook.issue: World Aquatics commentary dated 6 August 2026, PDF p. 1, explicitly disapplies 3.3.5 and says it will be removed at the next annual revision. The row remains in the complete index so readers can understand the printed code.

rulebook.title: Seeding the final
rulebook.statement: At Olympic, World Aquatics and other competitions governed by these regulations, individual and relay final lanes are allocated by seeding under the provisions that follow.
rulebook.plain: Final lane assignments follow the applicable seeding and progression rules.

rulebook.title: Eight qualifiers for the final
rulebook.statement: The printed qualification rule selects the eight fastest swimmers using semi-final times, or entry times where the event is a direct final. Rules 3.4.2.2–3.4.2.3 provide the specific longer-distance exceptions that can expand a final to nine or ten swimmers.
rulebook.plain: Normally eight swimmers qualify for the final. The special longer-distance tie rules can admit extra swimmers when ten lanes are available.
rulebook.issue: This February provision expressly names semi-final times and direct-final entry times; it does not expressly state the qualifying-time basis for a heats-to-final event with no semi-final round. Rule 3.7.2 confirms that such formats exist. This entry does not silently replace the printed wording with an inferred formula.

rulebook.title: Tie for the last final place at 200m or shorter
rulebook.statement: For an event of 200m or less, swimmers tied in seeding for the final available final place may race a swim-off to determine who qualifies.
rulebook.plain: A tie for the last final place at 50m, 100m or 200m may require a swim-off.

rulebook.title: Longer race: two tied for eighth with ten lanes
rulebook.statement: For an event longer than 200m, including a relay, if seven entrants already have final places and exactly two share the eighth-place seed, both tied entrants join the final when it is held in a ten-lane pool. Lane 0 is added, making nine finalists; a draw assigns the tied pair to lanes 8 and 0.
rulebook.plain: With two tied for eighth in a longer race and ten lanes available, both get a final place. Draw lanes 8 and 0 between them.

rulebook.title: Longer race: three tied for eighth with ten lanes
rulebook.statement: For an event longer than 200m, including a relay, if seven entrants already have final places and exactly three share the eighth-place seed, all three join the final when it is held in a ten-lane pool. Lanes 0 and 9 are added, making ten finalists; a draw assigns the tied three to lanes 8, 0 and 9.
rulebook.plain: With three tied for eighth in a longer race and ten lanes available, all three get a final place. Draw lanes 8, 0 and 9 between them.

rulebook.title: Longer race: more than three tied for eighth
rulebook.statement: For an event longer than 200m, including a relay, if seven entrants already have final places in a ten-lane pool and more than three share the eighth-place seed, a swim-off may be used to resolve qualification.
rulebook.plain: If more than three swimmers or teams tie for the last place in this longer-race situation, officials may arrange a swim-off.

rulebook.title: Longer-race ties without a ten-lane pool
rulebook.statement: If the longer-distance tie situations described in 3.4.2.2–3.4.2.4 arise but a ten-lane pool is unavailable, a swim-off may be used instead of the additional-lane arrangement.
rulebook.plain: Without ten lanes, those longer-distance ties may require a swim-off.

rulebook.title: Replacing a withdrawn finalist
rulebook.statement: If a finalist withdraws, the management committee gives the place to the fastest previously unqualified swimmer when it considers this reasonably possible. When a replacement is made, it re-ranks and re-seeds the final and allocates lanes again under 3.4.4.
rulebook.plain: A withdrawal may admit the next-fastest reserve. If that happens, the final is re-seeded.

rulebook.title: Assigning final lanes
rulebook.statement: Use the centre-outwards lane order specified in 3.2.5.1. If semi-finals took place, rank swimmers by their official semi-final times rather than the times submitted with their entries. If no semi-finals took place, the printed rule directs officials to 3.2.5.1.
rulebook.plain: Use the normal centre-out lane order for the final, with semi-final times determining the order where semi-finals were held.
rulebook.issue: For a format with heats but no semi-finals, this clause points to the lane-order provision 3.2.5.1 without expressly naming the ranking-time basis. The explanation retains that printed limit instead of inventing missing words.

rulebook.title: Relay final seeding: printed reference needs care
rulebook.statement: The printed relay-final provision says to apply 3.3.1–3.3.4 with each relay team treated as an entrant. Those cited clauses describe semi-finals, so the cross-reference does not provide a clear, self-contained relay-final allocation procedure. This entry preserves the reference and identifies the inconsistency rather than replacing it with an unverified correction.
rulebook.plain: This printed relay-final code points to semi-final instructions. The cross-reference is inconsistent; it should not be used to invent a second relay-final race or a relay semi-final round.
rulebook.issue: The February PDF cites 3.3.1–3.3.4 for relay finals. The archived 6 August commentary withdraws relay semi-finals at 3.3.5 but does not correct 3.4.5. No corrected target for this reference has been independently established in this review. Consult the event’s published progression arrangements or the responsible officials for this unresolved detail.

rulebook.title: Reporting to the call rooms
rulebook.statement: For Olympic and World Aquatics heats, semi-finals and finals, swimmers must attend the first call room at the time set by the management committee. After the inspection, they move to the final call room.
rulebook.plain: At these events, report at the stated call-room time, complete the checks and then proceed to the final call room.

rulebook.title: Drawn lanes outside this seeding framework
rulebook.statement: Competitions outside the Olympics, World Aquatics events and other events governed by the Competition Regulations may allocate lanes by a draw.
rulebook.plain: Outside the specified World Aquatics rules framework, a competition may draw lane positions.

rulebook.title: 25m World and Junior Championships: 50m and 100m rounds
rulebook.statement: At the World Aquatics Swimming Championships (25m) and the World Aquatics Junior Swimming Championships, 50m and 100m events have heats, semi-finals and finals.
rulebook.plain: At these two championships, 50m and 100m use three rounds.

rulebook.title: 25m World and Junior Championships: 200m and longer rounds
rulebook.statement: At the World Aquatics Swimming Championships (25m) and the World Aquatics Junior Swimming Championships, events of at least 200m have heats and finals only, with no semi-final round.
rulebook.plain: At these two championships, 200m and longer events go from heats to the final.

rulebook.title: 800m and 1500m may use timed finals at these championships
rulebook.statement: At the World Aquatics Swimming Championships (25m) and World Aquatics Junior Swimming Championships, the management committee may choose timed finals for 800m and 1500m freestyle. If it does, only the fastest heat is scheduled in the finals session.
rulebook.plain: Officials may run 800m and 1500m freestyle as timed finals, with only the fastest heat in the finals session.

rulebook.title: Races with a dive start
rulebook.statement: A dive is the required standard start for freestyle, breaststroke, butterfly and individual medley.
rulebook.plain: These four race types start from the block.

rulebook.title: Whistles before a dive start
rulebook.statement: After competitors have removed clothing other than their swimwear, several short referee whistles call them to prepare at the starting end. The following long whistle instructs them to mount the platforms and stay there.
rulebook.plain: Get ready at the short whistles; step onto your block at the long whistle.

rulebook.title: Referee hands control to the starter
rulebook.statement: Once competitors and officials are ready, the referee extends an arm to transfer control of the competitors to the starter. The arm remains extended until the race-start signal.
rulebook.plain: The referee’s raised arm shows that the starter is now controlling the start.

rulebook.title: Starting position on the platform
rulebook.statement: The instruction to take starting marks requires an immediate move into the starting stance. A minimum of one foot must touch the platform’s front edge. There is no prescribed placement for the hands.
rulebook.plain: At “take your marks”, get into position with at least one foot at the front of the block.

rulebook.title: Stillness before the signal
rulebook.statement: The starter gives the race-start signal when every competitor is stationary (still).
rulebook.plain: Settle and stay still while waiting for the signal.

rulebook.title: Races with an in-water start
rulebook.statement: Backstroke and medley relay races require a start from within the pool.
rulebook.plain: Backstroke starts in the water, including the first leg of a medley relay.

rulebook.title: First long whistle for an in-water start
rulebook.statement: Once competitors have removed clothing other than swimwear, several short referee whistles call them to prepare at the starting end. The following long whistle instructs them to enter the pool immediately.
rulebook.plain: For backstroke, enter the water at the first long whistle.

rulebook.title: Second long whistle for an in-water start
rulebook.statement: A second long whistle from the referee instructs competitors to reach their starting positions promptly.
rulebook.plain: At the second long whistle, come straight to your starting position.

rulebook.title: Referee hands control over for an in-water start
rulebook.statement: Once competitors and officials are ready, the referee extends an arm to put the competitors under the starter’s control and keeps it extended until the race-start signal.
rulebook.plain: The referee’s arm tells you the starter is now in charge.

rulebook.title: Marks command for an in-water start
rulebook.statement: The starter instructs competitors to take their marks after everyone has adopted the backstroke starting position required by rule 6.1.
rulebook.plain: Set yourself at the wall with the correct hand and foot position, then follow the marks command.

rulebook.title: Stillness for an in-water start
rulebook.statement: The starter gives the race-start signal when every competitor is stationary (still).
rulebook.plain: Stay still in your starting position until the signal.

rulebook.title: Commands at World Aquatics events
rulebook.statement: At Olympic Games, World Aquatics Championships and other World Aquatics events, the marks instruction is given in English. Speakers at each starting platform carry the commands and start signal.
rulebook.plain: At these international events, listen for the English marks command through the speaker by your block.

rulebook.title: Starting before the signal
rulebook.statement: Initiating the start before the race-start signal is grounds for disqualification.
rulebook.plain: Wait for the signal before beginning your start; an early start can mean a DQ.

rulebook.title: Early start discovered after the signal
rulebook.statement: If the race-start signal has already sounded before an early-start disqualification is announced, competitors continue racing. The disqualification is imposed when the race ends.
rulebook.plain: Keep racing if the signal has sounded; an early starter can be disqualified afterwards.

rulebook.title: Early start declared before the signal
rulebook.statement: If an early-start disqualification is announced before the signal, the starter does not start the race. Remaining competitors are told to stand down, then the referee restarts the procedure at the appropriate long whistle: rule 4.1.1 for a dive start or 4.2.2 for an in-water start.
rulebook.plain: If officials stop the start before the signal, stand down and follow the repeated starting procedure.

rulebook.title: Which strokes freestyle permits
rulebook.statement: A freestyle event allows any swimming style. The freestyle section of an individual medley or medley relay excludes backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly.
rulebook.plain: Freestyle usually means you may choose any stroke. In medley freestyle, you must use something other than the other three strokes.

rulebook.title: Freestyle wall contact
rulebook.statement: Completion of every length, including the last, requires contact between the wall and some part of the swimmer’s body.
rulebook.plain: Touch the wall at every turn and at the finish. A hand is not the only body part that can count.

rulebook.title: Freestyle: head at the surface by 15 metres
rulebook.statement: After every start and turn, the head must already have broken the water surface no later than 15 metres from that wall. A first head breakout at 15.01 metres is too late. Full submersion (being completely submerged) is allowed during the turn and within that start/turn distance. Otherwise, some portion of the swimmer’s body must intersect the surface throughout the swim; rule 5.4 provides a separate finish exception.
rulebook.plain: Your head must break the surface by 15m, never beyond it. After breakout, keep some part of your body at the surface, subject to the separate turn and finish exceptions.

rulebook.title: Freestyle: submersion on the finish reach
rulebook.statement: Complete submersion (being completely submerged) is permitted when reaching for the final wall, but only after some portion of the head has passed the marker 5 metres from that wall. This is a finish-reaching exception, not general permission for an underwater final 5 metres.
rulebook.plain: Your head must be past the 5m marker and you must be reaching for the finish before you may be fully underwater.

rulebook.title: Backstroke starting grip and foot placement
rulebook.statement: Before the signal, the swimmer is in the pool looking towards the starting wall and holding the starting grips with both hands. The gutter cannot be used as a standing surface or hooked with the toes. If a backstroke ledge is used, each foot needs at least one toe touching the wall or the front face of the timing pad. Toes must not hook over the pad’s top.
rulebook.plain: Face the wall and hold both grips. With a ledge, keep a toe from each foot against the wall or pad face; do not hook your toes over the top.

rulebook.title: Backstroke body position
rulebook.statement: At the start signal and after each turn, the swimmer pushes away on the back and retains that orientation while swimming, apart from the turn allowed by rule 6.4. Body rotation towards either side must remain less than 90 degrees from horizontal. Head direction does not determine compliance.
rulebook.plain: Stay on your back. You can roll towards your side, but not reach or pass vertical during ordinary swimming.

rulebook.title: Backstroke: head at the surface by 15 metres
rulebook.statement: After every start and turn, the head must already have broken the water surface no later than 15 metres from that wall. Breaking out for the first time at 15.01 metres breaches the limit. Full submersion (being completely submerged) is allowed during the turn and within that start/turn distance. At other times, some portion of the body must intersect the surface, with the separate finish provision in rule 6.5.
rulebook.plain: Your head must break the surface by 15m. Keep part of your body at the surface afterwards unless a turn or the finish exception applies.

rulebook.title: Backstroke turn into another backstroke length
rulebook.statement: The turn requires wall contact by some part of the body. The shoulders may rotate beyond vertical towards the breast for the turn. If an arm action starts the turn, it must be an immediate, continuous pull with either one arm (a single-arm pull) or both arms simultaneously (a double-arm pull). The swimmer must be back on the back at wall departure. The turn must be initiated at completion of that pull, without a pause or glide on the breast.
rulebook.plain: Roll straight into your backstroke turn. If you use a pull, keep it continuous and start the turn when it finishes; do not pause or glide on your front. Touch the wall and push off on your back. A back-to-breast medley change needs a backstroke finish instead.

rulebook.title: Backstroke finish on the back
rulebook.statement: The final wall touch must occur with the swimmer still on the back. Complete submersion (being completely submerged) is allowed during the finish reach once the head has passed the marker 5 metres from the finish wall.
rulebook.plain: Touch the finish on your back. Being underwater can be legal during the finish reach after your head has passed 5m.

rulebook.title: Breaststroke pullout and breakout
rulebook.statement: After each start and turn, one underwater arm pull may extend as far as the legs. One optional butterfly kick is allowed before the first breaststroke kick. During the second arm stroke, the head must break the surface before the hands begin to sweep inward from their widest separation.
rulebook.plain: You may take one long pullout and one butterfly kick before your first breaststroke kick. Your head must surface before the inward sweep of the second pull.

rulebook.title: Breaststroke body position from the first pull
rulebook.statement: From the beginning of the first arm stroke after a start or turn, the swimmer’s body must be on the breast during the swim. Rule 7.3 sets out the no-roll requirement and the turn exception, including the separately flagged later kick clarification.
rulebook.plain: Be on your breast from your first pull onwards. Read 7.3 for what changes at a turn.

rulebook.title: Breaststroke cycle and orientation after a turn
rulebook.statement: Ordinary breaststroke swimming does not allow a roll onto the back. After a legal turn touch, rotation may be in any direction, with breast orientation restored by the start of the first arm stroke following departure. Throughout the race, each stroke cycle uses an arm action followed by a leg kick, and both arms act simultaneously, rather than alternating. The August World Aquatics commentary also requires rotation past vertical towards the breast before any kick after the turn.
rulebook.plain: Swim pull, then kick, with both arms working together. Turn freely after touching; the latest World Aquatics guidance says get past your side towards your breast before kicking.
rulebook.issue: February rule: body on the breast by the first arm stroke after departure. World Aquatics commentary dated 6 August 2026, p. 2, additionally requires return past vertical towards the breast before a post-turn kick. Application of that August clarification in England has not been independently confirmed. The current World Aquatics interpretation is shown, with this local-applicability issue flagged.

rulebook.title: Breaststroke arm path and elbows
rulebook.statement: The hands travel forward simultaneously from the chest and may pass below, at or above the water. Elbows normally remain submerged; exceptions cover the last stroke into a turn, the turn itself and the last stroke into the finish. The backward hand movement stays at or below the surface and must stop by the hip line, except on the first stroke following a start or turn.
rulebook.plain: Send both hands forward together. Keep elbows underwater except at the listed turn and finish moments. Only the first pull after a start or turn may go past your hips.

rulebook.title: Breaststroke head and leg timing
rulebook.statement: Every completed stroke cycle requires some portion of the head to break the water surface. The two legs must move simultaneously; alternating leg actions are prohibited.
rulebook.plain: Bring your head through the surface in each full cycle, and move both legs together.

rulebook.title: Breaststroke kick shape
rulebook.statement: During the kick’s propulsive phase, the feet are turned outwards. Alternating kicks are prohibited, as are downward butterfly kicks other than the single allowance in rule 7.1. Feet may emerge through the surface provided they are not then used for a downward butterfly kick.
rulebook.plain: Turn your feet out for the push. Do not flutter kick or add butterfly kicks; the one allowed pullout kick is the exception.

rulebook.title: Breaststroke touch and last cycle
rulebook.statement: Every turn and finish requires both hands to contact the wall simultaneously. The hands must be separated, meaning that one hand must not be stacked on the other. The touch can be above, at or below the surface. A visible gap is unnecessary and incidental finger contact is acceptable. The final arm stroke into either wall may omit its following kick. The head may go underwater after that last pull if it surfaced during the final full or partial cycle before contact.
rulebook.plain: Touch with two hands together in time, but not stacked. You may finish the last pull without a kick and dip your head after it, provided your head surfaced during that final cycle.

rulebook.title: Butterfly position when the first pull starts
rulebook.statement: For the start of a butterfly swim, breast orientation is required from the moment the first arm action begins. The February provision also mentions turns, but the August World Aquatics commentary removes turns from this clause and directs turn departures to the stricter requirement in rule 8.2.
rulebook.plain: After the start, be on your breast when your first pull begins. For a turn, use the separately flagged departure rule 8.2.
rulebook.issue: World Aquatics commentary dated 6 August 2026, p. 2, removes the turn reference from 8.1. Its application in England has not been independently confirmed. This row explains the current World Aquatics reading and preserves the distinction from February wording.

rulebook.title: Butterfly orientation when leaving the turn
rulebook.statement: Rolling onto the back is prohibited during ordinary butterfly swimming. After touching for a turn, the swimmer may rotate in any direction. Under the August World Aquatics interpretation, the swimmer must have breast orientation on leaving the wall; waiting until the first arm action is not sufficient under that interpretation.
rulebook.plain: After your turn touch, turn around and leave the wall on your breast under the latest World Aquatics guidance.
rulebook.issue: The February printed clause sets breast orientation at the first arm stroke after departure. World Aquatics commentary dated 6 August 2026, p. 2, instead sets the requirement at departure from the wall. England’s application of this August clarification has not been independently confirmed; the difference is material and remains flagged.

rulebook.title: Butterfly arm movement
rulebook.statement: Butterfly uses simultaneous arm actions: both arms recover forward together above the water, then pull backwards together underwater. The special underwater arm action in rule 8.6 is the exception to this pattern.
rulebook.plain: Recover both arms over the water together and pull underwater together.

rulebook.title: Butterfly leg movement
rulebook.statement: The upward and downward leg movements must be simultaneous. Unequal leg or foot heights are allowed, but alternating their relative positions is not. A breaststroke-type kick is prohibited.
rulebook.plain: Dolphin-kick with both legs together. Your feet can be at slightly different heights, but cannot alternate or make a breaststroke kick.

rulebook.title: Butterfly turn and finish touch
rulebook.statement: Every turn and finish requires both hands to meet the wall simultaneously. The hands must be separated, meaning that one hand must not be stacked on the other. Contact may be at, above or below the surface. There is no requirement for a visible space between the hands, and incidental finger contact is allowed.
rulebook.plain: Touch with both hands at the same time. They must not be stacked; different heights or a little finger contact can be legal.

rulebook.title: Butterfly underwater limit and finish exception
rulebook.statement: Following a start or turn, completely submerged swimming may include one or more leg kicks and a single arm pull; that pull must bring the swimmer to the surface. The head must already have broken the surface no later than 15 metres from the wall: a first breakout at 15.01 metres is late. Some part of the body otherwise remains at the surface, apart from the turn itself and a finish reach after the head has passed the 5-metre marker.
rulebook.plain: One underwater pull must bring you up, and your head must break the surface by 15m. Do not swim a second underwater pull. The last reach to finish has its own 5m exception.

rulebook.title: Individual medley stroke order
rulebook.statement: Individual medley assigns one quarter of the full distance to each stroke: butterfly first, then backstroke, then breaststroke, then freestyle.
rulebook.plain: IM goes fly, back, breast, free, with equal distances.

rulebook.title: Medley relay stroke order
rulebook.statement: A medley relay assigns one quarter of the full distance to each stroke: backstroke first, then breaststroke, then butterfly, then freestyle.
rulebook.plain: Medley relay goes back, breast, fly, free, with one equal leg for each swimmer.

rulebook.title: Medley freestyle orientation and turn departure
rulebook.statement: During the freestyle quarter of either type of medley, the swimmer maintains breast orientation except during a turn. Departure from a turn on the back is allowed, but rotation beyond vertical towards the breast must occur before any kick or arm stroke. After that rotation, one or more butterfly kicks are permitted.
rulebook.plain: In medley freestyle, you may push off on your back, but roll past your side towards your breast before kicking or pulling.

rulebook.title: Changing strokes in medley
rulebook.statement: Each quarter ends using the finish requirements of the stroke that is being completed.
rulebook.plain: Finish the outgoing stroke legally before changing stroke. For back to breast, touch while still on your back; a normal backstroke tumble turn is not a substitute.

rulebook.title: Individual competition categories
rulebook.statement: Individual events are organised as separate male and female competitions under these regulations.
rulebook.plain: These regulations separate the men’s and women’s individual events.

rulebook.title: Complete the required distance
rulebook.statement: An individual competitor must cover the event’s full distance; a relay swimmer must cover their own quarter of the total.
rulebook.plain: Swim the whole race, or your whole relay leg.

rulebook.title: Use the allocated lane
rulebook.statement: The assigned lane is compulsory for the start, the full swim and the finish.
rulebook.plain: Stay in your allocated lane from start to finish.

rulebook.title: Turn contact and no step from the bottom
rulebook.statement: A turn requires body contact with the wall at the end of the course. The swimmer cannot step or stride from the pool floor. The freestyle standing exception in rule 10.2.4 does not permit walking.
rulebook.plain: Touch the end wall to turn; do not step along or push forward by striding off the pool bottom.

rulebook.title: Standing and walking on the pool floor
rulebook.statement: Standing or walking on the pool floor is prohibited. Freestyle events and the freestyle quarter of medley permit standing only; walking remains prohibited.
rulebook.plain: Only freestyle allows you to stand on the bottom. You still cannot walk.

rulebook.title: No pulling the lane rope
rulebook.statement: Using the lane rope to pull oneself along is prohibited.
rulebook.plain: Do not pull yourself forward on the lane rope.

rulebook.title: Do not obstruct another swimmer
rulebook.statement: A competitor must not obstruct or impede another competitor or otherwise interfere with their swim.
rulebook.plain: Give other swimmers a clear race; do not get in their way.

rulebook.title: No entry during somebody else’s race
rulebook.statement: A person who is not a competitor in the race must stay out of the pool until every swimmer in that race has covered the required distance.
rulebook.plain: Do not jump into someone else’s race, even if the first swimmers have finished.

rulebook.title: Leave after finishing without interference
rulebook.statement: After completing the required distance, a swimmer must get out as promptly as possible while avoiding obstruction or interference with anyone still completing the swim.
rulebook.plain: Clear the pool promptly and safely without disturbing swimmers who are still racing.

rulebook.title: No pacemaking
rulebook.statement: Acting or attempting to act as a pacemaker is prohibited: a swimmer may neither provide nor attempt to provide pacing for another competitor. Using or attempting to use a pacing device or pacing arrangement is also prohibited.
rulebook.plain: Do not pace another swimmer or use a pacing device or plan.

rulebook.title: Disqualification for general race breaches
rulebook.statement: The referee decides whether a requirement in 10.2 has been breached. A confirmed breach results in disqualification from the event, except that an unauthorised entry under 10.2.7 disqualifies the entering swimmer from their next scheduled race at the competition.
rulebook.plain: Breaking these general race rules can remove you from the result. Jumping into someone else’s race carries the penalty in your next race.

rulebook.title: Deliberate interference and disciplinary reporting
rulebook.statement: If interference under 10.2.6 appears intentional, the referee must inform the management committee. The committee reports it to the host-country federation and the swimmer’s federation as appropriate for possible investigation and discipline. The Aquatics Integrity Unit can also act on World Aquatics event incidents; the relevant authority can act at other competitions.
rulebook.plain: Deliberately interfering with a swimmer can lead to action beyond the race disqualification.

rulebook.title: Relay team size and mixed teams
rulebook.statement: A relay team consists of four swimmers. In a mixed relay, that four must comprise two men and two women.
rulebook.plain: Relays use four swimmers; a mixed relay uses two men and two women.

rulebook.title: Declare the relay order
rulebook.statement: The team leader must specify and submit the swimmers’ racing order before the management committee’s stated deadline. The team must compete in that declared order.
rulebook.plain: Submit your team order before the deadline, then swim in that order.

rulebook.title: Late relay substitutions
rulebook.statement: After the order deadline, changing one relay swimmer for another requires a documented medical emergency and advance approval from the referee, World Aquatics technical delegate or management committee, as applicable.
rulebook.plain: A late swimmer change needs evidence of a medical emergency and permission first.

rulebook.title: Changing the team for a relay final
rulebook.statement: The team’s members may differ between heats and finals, provided each chosen swimmer is eligible for that relay event at the competition.
rulebook.plain: You may change the eligible swimmers between the relay heat and final.

rulebook.title: One relay leg per swimmer
rulebook.statement: A competitor cannot appear more than once in the same relay race.
rulebook.plain: Each swimmer does one leg only.

rulebook.title: Relay exchange departure point
rulebook.statement: A relay takeover begins on the starting platform. Starting with a run-up (a running start) from the surrounding pool deck is prohibited.
rulebook.plain: Start your takeover from the block; do not run in from poolside.

rulebook.title: Feet must retain block contact until the touch
rulebook.statement: The outgoing relay swimmer’s feet must retain contact with the starting platform until the incoming team member touches the wall at the end of their leg.
rulebook.plain: You may move before the touch, but do not lose foot contact with the block until your teammate has touched.

rulebook.title: Relay team members entering the water
rulebook.statement: During a relay, only the team member whose leg is next may enter for their swim. Other team members must not enter or re-enter until every team’s competitors have completed the race distance.
rulebook.plain: Unless it is your turn to swim, stay out of the water until everyone has finished.

rulebook.title: Leaving the pool after a relay leg
rulebook.statement: A swimmer who has finished a relay leg must get out as promptly as possible without obstructing or interfering with anyone still swimming their leg.
rulebook.plain: Leave after your leg without getting in a racing swimmer’s way.

rulebook.title: Disqualification for a relay breach
rulebook.statement: If the referee finds that a swimmer or another person has breached a requirement in 10.4, the relay team is disqualified. If the offender is a swimmer, that swimmer is disqualified too.
rulebook.plain: A relay-rule breach can disqualify the whole team.

rulebook.title: Opportunity to swim again after interference
rulebook.statement: When a swimmer’s breach of 10.2 or 10.4 damages another swimmer’s or relay team’s chances, the referee may let the affected competitor or team race in the next heat. If the incident was in the last heat or a final, the referee may order that heat or final to be repeated. Both the finding and remedy are at the referee’s discretion.
rulebook.plain: If someone else’s breach spoils your race, the referee may give you another swim; it is not automatic.

rulebook.title: Rules when electronic timing is used
rulebook.statement: The requirements in 11.1 apply when automatic officiating equipment is used and, where relevant, when semi-automatic equipment is used.
rulebook.plain: Use the electronic-timing provisions for an electronically timed race; the separate rules in 11.2 cover races without either system.

rulebook.title: Officials supervise the timing system
rulebook.statement: The officials appointed for this role must oversee operation of the automatic officiating equipment.
rulebook.plain: Electronic timing remains under official supervision.

rulebook.title: Electronic times determine placings
rulebook.statement: The automatic system must record each competitor’s time for the full course and establish the winner and other placings from those times. Matching times produce matching placings.
rulebook.plain: Equal recorded times mean a tie; a separate visual impression does not by itself break it.

rulebook.title: Electronic timing takes priority when functioning
rulebook.statement: Automatic times and the placings derived from them are presumed correct and take priority over manual times or Finish Judges’ placings. The Control Room Supervisor must tell the Referee that the automatic equipment suffered no malfunction, breakdown or failure during the race.
rulebook.plain: The electronic result is the first reference, with the required check that the equipment worked. If it failed, the following backup procedures apply.

rulebook.title: Electronic timing accuracy
rulebook.statement: Automatic equipment must record race times accurately to 0.01 seconds.
rulebook.plain: Timing accuracy is one hundredth of a second.

rulebook.title: Electronic results displayed to hundredths
rulebook.statement: Every output of the race result, including the venue scoreboard and official result reports, must display times to hundredths of a second.
rulebook.plain: The public display and the official results must use the same two-decimal precision.

rulebook.title: Recovering placings after electronic failure
rulebook.statement: If automatic equipment does not record a time, a placing, or both for one or more competitors, the Referee must gather the available evidence and determine official placings under 11.1.6.1–11.1.6.2.3.
rulebook.plain: A missed electronic result triggers the prescribed backup procedure; it does not mean inventing a time or ignoring the remaining valid electronic results.

rulebook.title: Gather all available timing evidence
rulebook.statement: After the relevant automatic recording failure, the Referee must assemble every available time and placing from the automatic system, Timekeepers and any appointed Finish Judges.
rulebook.plain: Collect the electronic and official manual evidence before reconstructing the result.

rulebook.title: Determine official placings after a failure
rulebook.statement: The Referee must establish the official order using the three cases in 11.1.6.2.1–11.1.6.2.3, according to the automatic information available for each competitor.
rulebook.plain: The method depends on whether that swimmer has both an electronic time and placing, a time alone, or neither.

rulebook.title: Preserve order between valid automatic results
rulebook.statement: Competitors with both an automatic time and an automatic placing must keep their relative order against every other competitor in that race who also has both records.
rulebook.plain: Filling a gap in the result must not swap the order of swimmers whose complete automatic results are valid.

rulebook.title: Automatic time available but placing missing
rulebook.statement: If a competitor has an automatic time but no automatic placing, determine the placing by comparing that time with the automatic times of competitors who have both automatic times and placings in the same race.
rulebook.plain: A valid electronic time can be used to put that swimmer into the finishing order even if the placing field is missing.

rulebook.title: No automatic time or placing available
rulebook.statement: Where no automatic time or placing is available for a competitor, determine the placing by comparing the semi-automatic or Timekeepers’ time with the times of competitors in that race who have both automatic times and placings.
rulebook.plain: Use the permitted backup time to fit the swimmer into the remaining valid electronic result.

rulebook.title: Official times after electronic failure
rulebook.statement: When automatic equipment misses a time or placing for one or more swimmers, assign each official time using 11.1.7.1 and 11.1.7.2.
rulebook.plain: The decision about the official time is separate from reconstructing the placing.

rulebook.title: Keep an available automatic time
rulebook.statement: If the automatic equipment recorded a competitor’s time, that recorded time is the official time.
rulebook.plain: A missing placing does not discard a valid automatic time.

rulebook.title: Use backup when the automatic time is missing
rulebook.statement: If the automatic equipment did not record a competitor’s time, the official time must come from semi-automatic equipment or the Timekeepers.
rulebook.plain: Use the recognised backup source for a missing electronic time.

rulebook.title: Rules without electronic officiating equipment
rulebook.statement: The provisions in 11.2 apply when neither automatic nor semi-automatic officiating equipment is used.
rulebook.plain: These are the rules for a race timed by the appointed Timekeepers without either electronic officiating system.

rulebook.title: Manual times determine placings
rulebook.statement: Timekeepers must record the competitors’ course times, and the Referee must use those times to establish the winner and placings. Competitors with matching times receive the same placing.
rulebook.plain: In this timing arrangement, equal official manual times remain tied.

rulebook.title: Approved Timekeepers and accurate devices
rulebook.statement: Each Timekeeper must be appointed or approved by the member federation of the host country. Every watch or other timing device must have accuracy certification satisfactory to that federation.
rulebook.plain: Both the person timing and the accuracy of their device need the required federation acceptance.

rulebook.title: Two Timekeepers for each manual time
rulebook.statement: Two Timekeepers must record each competitor’s course time to hundredths of a second. The official time is then determined using the comparison and failure procedures in 11.2.3.1–11.2.3.3.
rulebook.plain: Take two independent times and use the specified method, rather than choosing whichever result is preferred.

rulebook.title: Average differing watches without rounding
rulebook.statement: If the two watches disagree, the official time is their average. When the average has a third decimal place, discard that final digit; do not apply a rounding adjustment.
rulebook.plain: For example, 60.01 and 60.02 seconds average to 60.015, which is recorded as 60.01 seconds, not 60.02.

rulebook.title: One watch fails
rulebook.statement: If one of the two timing devices fails, use the time shown by the device that worked as the official time.
rulebook.plain: One functioning official watch supplies the time when its partner fails.

rulebook.title: Both watches fail
rulebook.statement: If neither watch produces a usable time because both have failed, a reswim may be offered to the competitor.
rulebook.plain: A reswim is permitted here, but this clause does not make it automatic.

rulebook.title: Manual results displayed to hundredths
rulebook.statement: All outputs of manually timed race results must present times to hundredths of a second.
rulebook.plain: Publish the official manual time with two decimal places.

rulebook.title: Individual disqualification in the results
rulebook.statement: An individual-race or individual-event disqualification must appear in the official results. No time or placing for that performance may be recorded or announced.
rulebook.plain: The result records the disqualification instead of giving the disqualified swim a time and placing.

rulebook.title: Relay disqualification and earlier legal splits
rulebook.statement: A disqualification during or after a relay must be shown in the official results, without a relay time or placing being recorded or announced. However, legal splits achieved by teammates before the disqualified swimmer participated must remain in the official results.
rulebook.plain: A relay disqualification removes the team result, while the specifically permitted earlier legal splits are retained.

rulebook.title: Publish the first relay swimmer’s splits
rulebook.statement: The automatic system, semi-automatic system or Timekeepers, as applicable, must record the first swimmer’s 50 m and 100 m relay splits and publish those splits in the official results.
rulebook.plain: The first leg’s applicable 50 m and 100 m split readings are part of the published results; a split can only exist for a distance that swimmer completes.

rulebook.title: Combine heats by official time
rulebook.statement: Rank competitors across the combined heats by their official times. Matching official times share the placing. In a displayed list, tied competitors are ordered by descending lane number, with alphabetical order used if the lane numbers are also equal.
rulebook.plain: Swimmers in different heats are compared by time. The listing order for tied names does not remove the tie.

rulebook.title: World-record events in a 50 m pool
rulebook.statement: World and World Junior Records are recognised in 50 m pools for both sexes in these events: freestyle 50, 100, 200, 400, 800 and 1500 m; backstroke 50, 100 and 200 m; breaststroke 50, 100 and 200 m; butterfly 50, 100 and 200 m; individual medley 200 and 400 m; freestyle relays 4 × 100 and 4 × 200 m; medley relay 4 × 100 m. The mixed relay categories are 4 × 100 m freestyle and 4 × 100 m medley.
rulebook.plain: The long-course record programme includes those distances and relay combinations. It does not include a 100 m individual medley or 4 × 50 m relay category under this clause.

rulebook.title: World-record events in a 25 m pool
rulebook.statement: World and World Junior Records are recognised in 25 m pools for both sexes in these events: freestyle 50, 100, 200, 400, 800 and 1500 m; backstroke 50, 100 and 200 m; breaststroke 50, 100 and 200 m; butterfly 50, 100 and 200 m; individual medley 100, 200 and 400 m; freestyle relays 4 × 50, 4 × 100 and 4 × 200 m; medley relays 4 × 50 and 4 × 100 m. The mixed relay categories are 4 × 50 m freestyle and 4 × 50 m medley.
rulebook.plain: The short-course programme adds 100 m individual medley and 4 × 50 m relays. Its listed mixed-relay record events are 4 × 50 m, unlike the 4 × 100 m long-course list.

rulebook.title: Record eligibility requires all relevant rules
rulebook.statement: A proposed World Record or World Junior Record must comply with every relevant World Aquatics rule, including these competition regulations and the requirements listed under 12.3. The listed criteria are not exhaustive.
rulebook.plain: A fast enough time alone is insufficient; all applicable record requirements must be met.

rulebook.title: Permitted swimwear for a record
rulebook.statement: For record eligibility, the swimmer must have worn only swimwear permitted under Part One, Article 6.
rulebook.plain: Record eligibility depends on compliance with the official swimwear requirements.

rulebook.title: World Junior Record age window
rulebook.statement: A World Junior Record applicant must be aged 14, 15, 16, 17 or 18 on 31 December of the calendar year in which the performance occurred.
rulebook.plain: The junior-record age test uses the end of the performance year, not the swimmer’s age on race day.

rulebook.title: One sporting nationality for a record relay
rulebook.statement: Every member of a relay claiming a World Record or World Junior Record must share the same sporting nationality as determined by Part One, Article 3.
rulebook.plain: A record relay must meet the common sporting-nationality requirement; this app does not add a separate nationality test.

rulebook.title: Individual record from a relay lead-off
rulebook.statement: Only the swimmer covering the first quarter of a relay may claim an individual World Record or World Junior Record from that relay. If that swimmer is not disqualified, their performance remains eligible when the team is disqualified for a reason arising or identified after that swimmer has finished.
rulebook.plain: An eligible first-leg swim can stand as an individual record even if a later team problem disqualifies the relay, provided the lead-off swimmer is not themselves disqualified.

rulebook.title: Match or improve the existing record
rulebook.statement: The performance must be at least as fast as the existing World Record or World Junior Record.
rulebook.plain: Equalling the current record can qualify; a slower swim cannot.

rulebook.title: Equal record time and joint holders
rulebook.statement: A swimmer who equals the existing record to hundredths of a second may apply to be recognised as a joint holder of that World Record or World Junior Record.
rulebook.plain: Matching the official record time can earn shared record-holder status.

rulebook.title: One winner when several swimmers beat a record
rulebook.statement: If several swimmers in a race equal or improve the existing record but there is a single winner, only that winner may apply for record recognition, unless the World Junior Record exception in 12.3.5.3 applies.
rulebook.plain: Beating the old record in the same race as a faster eligible winner does not normally give the runner-up that record.

rulebook.title: Junior-record exception for a nonwinner
rulebook.statement: A swimmer who equals or improves the World Junior Record without winning may apply for that junior record if no better-placed swimmer who is eligible for it also set a World Junior Record in the race.
rulebook.plain: A junior can set the junior record while finishing behind an older swimmer, provided no better-placed eligible junior has also achieved the record.

rulebook.title: Joint winners and record recognition
rulebook.statement: If several swimmers win a race jointly and equal or improve the existing World Record or World Junior Record, every joint winner may apply for recognition of the qualifying record performance.
rulebook.plain: A tie for first can produce joint record holders.

rulebook.title: Intermediate-distance record requires the full race
rulebook.statement: A split at an intermediate distance in an individual race may qualify for a record, but the swimmer must complete the entire entered race distance. Stopping after the record split or at any shorter distance does not meet this requirement.
rulebook.plain: A swimmer seeking a record at an intermediate split must still finish the longer race.

rulebook.title: Conditions surrounding a record performance
rulebook.statement: The record attempt must satisfy the timing, water, event and pool-measurement conditions specified in 12.3.7.1–12.3.7.5.
rulebook.plain: The setting and verification of the swim matter as well as the recorded time.

rulebook.title: Electronic timing required for a record
